newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia marks space holiday in grim mood.
newsitem.headline: Russia marks space holiday in grim mood.

text.p: Russia marked the 36th anniversary of the first manned space flight, once one of its most celebrated state holidays, on Saturday with doubts hanging over the future of its space programme.

"(It) has become a sad holiday full of nostalgia," commented the liberal daily Komsomolskaya Pravda, one of the few Russian newspapers which commemorated the holiday established to mark Yuri Gagarin's space flight in 1961.
"Hard to believe, but we are no longer the first in the space and there are strong doubts about whether we will be able to become the first once again," the newspaper said.
Gagarin's mission was the crowning glory of Moscow's space programme, driven for decades by fierce competition with Washington.

Since the end of the Cold War, Russia and the United States have switched from rivalry to cooperation but Moscow's huge financial problems threaten its space programme and plans of cooperation with the West.

Colonel-General Vladimir Kovalyonok, a cosmonaut who now heads Russia's leading Zhukovsky air force academy, told the communist daily Pravda that the country had lost much of its scientific and technical potential.
He said Russia had lost nearly half of its space researchers since 1989. He said those who were still working in the sector had to live on salaries which averaged 650,000 roubles ($115) a month.
A NASA astronaut painted a disturbing picture on Friday of life on Moscow's 11-year-old Mir space station, now manned by a Russian-U.S. crew.

Speaking from space, Jerry Linenger said he and his two Russian colleagues had almost abandoned ship twice in the past few months and were making repairs to Mir's troubled cooling system in masks to avoid taking in toxic fumes from leaking coolant.
Temperatures and humidity aboard the station had soared when the cooling system failed and the crew were being forced to take parts from another device to fix Mir's main oxygen generators.
NASA officials said recently they would review safety aboard Mir -- the world's only space station -- before sending any more astronauts to live there.

President Boris Yeltsin told the head of the Russian Space Agency on Friday that the space programme "had fallen back from its achievements" since the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991 and urged him to press for more funds.
"Have you got a direct line to me?" Yeltsin asked Yuri Koptev. "Put one in," he said, gesturing to a waiting official.

Koptev said after the meeting that the government had promised money to allow him to fund part of Russia's contribution to the $37 billion Alpha International Space Station which is due to replace Mir by 2003.
Western officials had threatened to drop Russia from the project after it reneged on its commitments in February.
